newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers break taboo in "wild shoot-out".
newsitem.headline: German soldiers break taboo in "wild shoot-out".

text.p: German soldiers opened fire under "hostile conditions" for the first time since World War Two, in a spectacular operation to get Germans and other citizens out of Albania, German officials said on Friday.

Although the German army was reformed in the 1950s, the notorious militaristic past and memories of war-time atrocities committed in Nazi-occupied lands made active combat one the country's great post-war taboos.

That taboo has gradually been eroded since unification in 1990 with the deployment of Tornado jets in former Yugoslavia last year and this year's German contribution to the NATO-led peacekeeping SFOR mission in Bosnia.

And yet despite progress toward a normal military role -- German troops had never fired shots in the way they did to protect dozens of evacuees huddled together on a military airfield near Tirana from Albanian gunmen.

"The German Army has also had to use guns in Somalia to protect our soldiers, but this the first time they had to do so under hostile conditions," Defence Minister Volker Ruehe told a news conference referring to a United Nations peace-keeping mission in 1993.
Ruehe was speaking hours after German troops exchanged fire with Albanian gunmen during the perilous rescue of Western residents from a disused airfield outside Tirana.

Ruehe said he sent in five military helicopters from Bosnia protected by 25 soldiers to evacuate 120 people, mostly Germans and citizens of other European Union states, to Montenegro on Albania's northern border.
German military spokesmen Hartmut Bagger told the news conference that gunmen started shooting at evacuees as the third of five German military helicopters landed, and the German soldiers fired back.

"We could hear a wild shoot-out without knowing where the gunshot came from, who was shooting at whom and what sort of weapons they were using," Bagger said, describing how he could hear the battled over the line as he spoke with the German ambassador by mobile telephone.

Bagger said a crowd of Albanians had tried to storm the helicopter and that there was a bullet hole in one of the German helicopters. Bagger also said an Albanian had been lightly wounded but no foreigners were hurt.

Ruehe said he gave orders to shoot for protection if necessary after receiving consent from Bonn's main political parties in parliament. He said he was extremely pleased with the success of what was a dangerous and tricky mission.

"That (consent) is important because it was the first time we had such a situation in which it was clear the German government had to act and could act without a German parliament resolution," Ruehe said.
The 120 evacuees were due to arrive by plane at Cologne airport later on Friday.
